analysis.one_liner: Allows safe importation of cheaper prescription drugs and requires Medicare to negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in the Senate Health Committee with zero cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let Americans buy the same FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada, Australia, Japan, and other countries with equivalent safety standards, where prices are often far lower than in the United States. It sets up a registration and inspection system for importers and exporters, bans manufacturer tactics that block importation, and makes internet pharmacy sales subject to the same rules. Separately, it directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices directly with drug manufacturers on behalf of everyone enrolled in Medicare's Part D prescription drug plan.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and Americans who pay high prices for brand-name prescriptions. The bill's own findings note Americans pay up to five times more to fill prescriptions than consumers abroad, and that drug costs are 35 to 55 percent lower in other developed countries. Importation would let pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals buy those same drugs, and Medicare negotiation would push Part D prices down directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and people paying high drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Individuals could import up to a 90-day supply of a qualifying drug for personal use from a registered exporter, with a valid prescription and safety checks

Pharmacies, groups of pharmacies, and wholesalers could register as importers, subject to $10,000 registration fees, FDA inspections at least 12 times a year, chain-of-custody verification, and anti-counterfeiting markings

Manufacturers would be barred from discriminating against registered importers and exporters, cutting off or delaying supply, or making the foreign version of a drug different from the U.S. version to defeat importation

Reselling in the U.S. a prescription drug properly sold abroad would no longer count as patent infringement, and the Secretary would have to negotiate covered Part D drug prices with manufacturers for Part D and Medicare Advantage enrollees

The bill states Congress's finding that Americans pay up to five times more to fill prescriptions than consumers in other countries and that drug costs run 35 to 55 percent less in comparable developed countries

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face competition in their largest market from their own drugs sold cheaper abroad and would have their Medicare prices negotiated down by the government for the first time.

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs carry safety risks if standards slip; the bill responds with a heavy compliance regime — registered exporters must post bonds up to $1 million, FDA inspects facilities at least 12 times a year, and shipments must carry anti-counterfeiting markings — but the costs of policing that system fall on the FDA and are paid through fees on importers and exporters

The standard industry objection is that cutting U.S. drug prices through importation and negotiated Medicare prices would reduce revenue that funds research into new medicines; the bill rejects the price-control framing by arguing competitive pricing itself produces savings, but lower industry revenue would still have some effect on future drug development

The bill excludes several categories from importation — biologics like monoclonal antibodies, injected and infused drugs, and controlled substances — so many of the most expensive treatments would not be covered, limiting the savings

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential savings are real: Medicare Part D negotiation alone targets one of the largest drug markets in the world, and importation exposes U.S. prices to competition from countries where the same drugs cost far less. The costs are administrative — a new registration, inspection, and tracking system funded by fees — plus the unknown effect on future drug research. The biggest uncertainty is practical: the savings depend on manufacturers not finding ways around the anti-discrimination rules, and the bill's enforcement tools would be tested for the first time.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2010, referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Russell Feingold introduced the Fair Pricing for Prescription Drugs Act on May 25, 2010
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action was taken on it
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died in committee without a vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept U.S. prices unexposed to foreign competition and avoided Medicare price negotiation for another decade. Americans who pay high prescription prices, including Medicare beneficiaries, got none of the bill's savings.

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; drew no cosponsors

against.name: Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never took the bill up; it received no markup or vote before the Congress ended

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed drug importation and government negotiation of Medicare drug prices, and no member of either party in the Senate joined the bill

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call; its sponsor was a Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Importation would expose U.S. prices — the highest in the world per the bill's findings — to competition from identical drugs sold cheaper in Canada, Europe, Japan, and elsewhere, and Medicare negotiation would directly cut Part D prices. The bill also bans the supply cutoffs and product-differentiation tactics manufacturers have used to block importation.

industries.industry: Licensed pharmacies, wholesalers, and exporters in permitted countries
industries.note: The bill creates a registered importer and exporter system, letting Canadian and other foreign pharmacies and U.S. wholesalers lawfully sell lower-priced drugs to Americans under FDA oversight.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Government-negotiated drug prices would lower what these plans pay for drugs, but it would take setting prices out of their hands and hand it to the Secretary of Health and Human Services.
